This figure summarizes molecular design strategies for tuning the luminescence of organic emitters across both the single-molecule and aggregated states. At the molecular level, it shows how emission can be red-shifted by strengthening donor–acceptor interactions or extending conjugation, and how brightness can be improved through several structural modifications, including backbone distortion, intramolecular locking, ion–π interactions, shielding groups, and more planar building blocks. It also highlights ways to facilitate intersystem crossing, such as narrowing the singlet–triplet energy gap, increasing spin–orbit coupling with heavy atoms or lone-pair electrons, and using polymerization.

A separate theme is promoting thermal deactivation by introducing molecular rotors or enlarging the available motion space, implying increased nonradiative decay through motion. At the aggregation level, the figure emphasizes that emission depends strongly on how molecules pack: aggregates vary in compactness from loose to dense, in order from disordered to regular, and in size from small clusters to large particles. Finally, it shows that intermolecular or matrix interactions can be engineered through linkers, metallacycles, porous frameworks such as MOFs/COFs, or rigid host environments, all of which appear to control packing and excited-state behavior.
